---
title: Activation Checkpointing & Offloading
---

Activation checkpointing, activation offloading and layer offloading reduce GPU memory during
training. Each trades it for something else: extra compute, host memory, or PCIe bandwidth. The
first two are configured in one `activation_checkpointing` block; `layer_offloading`, which moves
parameters rather than activations, is a separate key.

### How it works

In the forward pass, each layer keeps some of its intermediate tensors (activations), because the
backward pass needs them to compute gradients. With long sequences these activations, not the
weights, take most of the GPU memory: they grow with batch size, sequence length, hidden size and
the number of layers.

- **Activation checkpointing** (`activation_checkpointing: true`) keeps only each decoder layer's
  input during forward and drops the rest. In backward, each layer runs its forward again
  (*recompute*) to rebuild what it needs. Memory drops to about one hidden-state tensor per layer,
  at the cost of roughly one extra forward pass per step.
- **Activation offloading** (`activation_checkpointing.offload`) keeps activations, but in CPU RAM
  until backward needs them: it spends PCIe bandwidth and host memory instead of compute.
- **Selective checkpointing** (`activation_checkpointing.selective`) recomputes each layer except
  for the ops it saves, attention by default, which is usually the most expensive part to
  recompute.

The block, with every field:

```yaml
activation_checkpointing:
  enabled: true              # recompute decoder layers in backward
  implementation: hf         # hf (transformers) | fsdp (FSDP2's checkpoint wrapper)
  reentrant: false           # use_reentrant; see below for the default
  kwargs:                    # extra torch.utils.checkpoint arguments
    every_n_layers: 2        # checkpoint every 2nd decoder layer only
  selective:                 # selective activation checkpointing (SAC)
    save: [attention]
  offload:                   # where each target's tensors go
    hidden_states: cpu       # each checkpointed layer's input
    selective: none          # what the selective policy saves
    all: none                # every saved activation (TRL's offloader)
```

`activation_checkpointing: true` turns on transformers' activation checkpointing with the defaults;
`false`, or leaving the key out, turns everything off. In the dict form `enabled` defaults to
`true`. Unknown fields in the block are rejected.

`offload` is a mapping, not a value. Each of its targets (`hidden_states`, `selective`, `all`) takes
`none` (the default), `cpu` or `disk`, and `true` / `false` mean `cpu` / `none`. `disk` is
rejected for now, pending a fix.

How recompute and offload placement combine (decoder layers; the output head always stays on GPU):

| `enabled` | `offload` | Recomputed in backward | Moved to CPU |
|---|---|---|---|
| `false` | — | nothing | nothing: every activation stays on GPU |
| `true` | — | every layer | nothing: each layer's input stays on GPU |
| `true` | `all: cpu` | every layer | each layer's input, and what is saved outside the layers |
| `false` | `all: cpu` | nothing | every saved activation |
| `true` | `hidden_states: cpu` | every layer | each layer's input only |

Adding `selective` skips recomputing the saved ops. Their outputs stay on GPU, or move to CPU with
`offload.selective: cpu`. For example, to offload each layer's input and not recompute attention:

```yaml
activation_checkpointing:
  selective:
    save: [attention]
  offload:
    hidden_states: cpu
    selective: cpu  # optional: keep the saved attention outputs in CPU RAM too
```

With `enabled: false`, only `offload.all` applies; setting `selective`, `offload.hidden_states`,
`offload.selective`, `reentrant`, `kwargs` or `implementation: fsdp` is an error rather than a silent
no-op.

### Enabling Activation Checkpointing

```yaml
activation_checkpointing: true
```

Unless `reentrant` is set, Axolotl uses PyTorch's recommended non-reentrant checkpointing
(`reentrant: false`). SFT runs on DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 default to `reentrant: true`, since
non-reentrant recompute raises a `CheckpointError` there; `rl:` runs on ZeRO-3 need it set
explicitly. Mistral Large 4, Gemma 4 and MixLoRA always run non-reentrant.

`kwargs` passes extra arguments to `torch.utils.checkpoint.checkpoint` (`preserve_rng_state`,
`determinism_check`, `debug`, `early_stop`), plus transformers' `every_n_layers`. Keys Axolotl sets
itself (`context_fn`, `respect_saved_tensors_hooks`), `offload` (use `offload.hidden_states`) and
anything torch does not accept are rejected: torch would pass an unknown key to each checkpointed
layer's forward, where it is ignored or overrides the layer's own argument.

#### FSDP2's checkpoint wrapper

```yaml
activation_checkpointing:
  implementation: fsdp
fsdp_config:
  ...
```

`implementation: fsdp` wraps each decoder layer in FSDP2's non-reentrant `checkpoint_wrapper`
instead of using transformers' checkpointing. transformers warns that its own checkpointing adds a
redundant all-gather in backward under FSDP. It requires `fsdp_config`, and the rest of the block
applies the same way: `selective` and `offload.selective` install the same save policy in the wrapper,
`offload.hidden_states` offloads each wrapped layer's input, `offload.all` runs TRL's offloader,
and `kwargs` (including `every_n_layers`) go to the wrapper. Only `reentrant: true` is rejected,
since the wrapper is non-reentrant. accelerate's own wrapper turns off `preserve_rng_state`; Axolotl
keeps torch's default (`true`), so dropout draws the same masks in the recompute. Set
`kwargs: {preserve_rng_state: false}` to skip saving the RNG state. DiffusionGemma, whose split checkpointing hooks transformers'
enable method, needs `implementation: hf`. Plugin-registered saves apply with either implementation.

### Enabling Activation Offloading

```yaml
activation_checkpointing:
  offload:
    all: cpu
```

With `offload.all: cpu`, `enabled` controls recompute:

- `true`: decoder layers are recomputed in backward; only tensors saved outside them are offloaded.
- `false`: nothing is recomputed and every saved activation is offloaded, bounded by host RAM and
  PCIe bandwidth. Can be faster for LoRA/QLoRA, whose activations are small. Not supported for
  ORPO, SimPO, EBFT or process reward models.

Activation offloading and selective checkpointing also apply to synchronous and async GRPO, whose
TRL trainers do not offload on their own.

Checkpointing runs exactly as it would without offloading, for adapters and full finetunes alike,
honoring `reentrant` and `kwargs`; the non-reentrant default above applies to `rl:` runs as well
(DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 stays reentrant).

`offload.all: cpu` offloads activations to CPU and uses CUDA streams to overlap the communications
and computations when offloading.

`offload.hidden_states: cpu` keeps checkpointing enabled and moves only the decoder-layer
checkpoint input (`hidden_states`) to CPU. With the default `reentrant: false`, Axolotl uses
Transformers' non-reentrant checkpointing plus a saved-tensor hook that only offloads marked
hidden-state tensors. Other saved tensors stay on GPU, which avoids the CPU memory and bandwidth
cost of full activation offload. It cannot be combined with `offload.all`, which already offloads
those tensors.

Set `reentrant: true` to use the older ALST-style implementation. That path patches torch's
reentrant `CheckpointFunction` and is DTensor-aware for sequence/context parallelism.

`disk` is accepted as a placement but rejected for now: disk offload is disabled pending a fix.

### Choosing a mode

| Mode | What moves | Best for |
|------|-----------|----------|
| `offload.all: cpu` | Saved activations → CPU, stream-overlapped | General use; LoRA/QLoRA without recompute (`enabled: false`) |
| `offload.hidden_states: cpu` | Per-layer checkpoint input only → CPU, stream-overlapped | Long-context training where full activation offload is CPU-memory or bandwidth-bound |

`offload.hidden_states` always recomputes each layer. For LoRA/QLoRA, `offload.all: cpu` with
`enabled: false` can be faster: adapter activations are small and pure offload skips recompute.

### Selective Activation Checkpointing (SAC)

```yaml
activation_checkpointing:
  selective: true
```

Plain activation checkpointing recomputes every op in a decoder layer during backward. Selective
checkpointing keeps the recompute for cheap ops but *saves* the outputs of expensive ones — by
default the attention op — so backward skips re-running them, for one extra hidden-state-sized
tensor per layer. Attention's backward and its first forward still run, so what this removes is
attention's share of the recompute. That share grows with the length each attention call spans:
on Qwen3-8B LoRA with full-length documents, saving attention sped steps up by about 2% at 8k
tokens and 9–15% at 32k (SDPA and flash-attention), for 2.3 GiB and 9.1 GiB of saved outputs. Rows
packed from short documents gain little, since each attention call spans one document. The
policy also runs Python for every op in the forward and the recompute, so on a slow host or a
small model that overhead can cost more than the saved attention.

This runs eagerly (no `torch.compile`) via torch's selective-checkpoint policy API. Ops are matched
at the dispatcher level: SDPA and flash-attention are matched out of the box, and custom kernels
that are not registered as torch ops are simply recomputed as usual — nothing breaks.

Flash Attention 4 (`attn_implementation: flash_attention_4`, or FA2/FA3 upgraded to it) is savable
too. FA4 (`flash_attn.cute`) registers no torch op, so inside checkpointed layers Axolotl runs it
through `axolotl::flash_attn_4_fwd` / `axolotl::flash_attn_4_varlen_fwd`. These call FA4's own
forward, and their backward calls FA4's own backward on the saved output and log-sum-exp, so the
kernels and numerics are unchanged and the backward does not re-run the attention forward.
Sliding-window FA4 calls are recognized from their window and recomputed like any other
(`save_sliding_window` applies), and `offload.selective: cpu` moves the saved FA4 outputs to CPU. FA4 calls
with attention sinks (`learnable_sink`) or mask/score mods, calls outside checkpointed layers and
calls under `torch.compile` go to FA4 directly and are recomputed as before. The
`kernels-community/flash-attn4` hub kernel is not covered: use `flash_attention_4` with
`flash-attn-4` installed.

The explicit form lets you save additional ops, matched as substrings of the qualified op name:

```yaml
activation_checkpointing:
  selective:
    save:
      - attention
      - aten::mm        # example: also save all matmuls
```

For hybrid models mixing full attention and sliding-window attention (SWA), only full-attention
calls are saved by default — SWA is cheap to recompute and not worth the memory. Hybrid layers are
detected two ways: the flash-attention window arguments, and the model's `layer_types` (published
per-layer via hooks, which also covers SDPA where the window lives inside the attention mask).
Set `selective.save_sliding_window: true` to save SWA calls too, or override which layer types
recompute with `selective.recompute_layer_types` (default
`[sliding_attention, chunked_attention]`; linear-attention layers never dispatch a matchable
attention op, so they need no entry).

To offload the saved tensors to pinned CPU memory instead of keeping them on GPU — asynchronous
side-stream copies during forward, prefetched back one region ahead during backward — set:

```yaml
activation_checkpointing:
  selective:
    save: [attention]
  offload:
    selective: cpu
```

This makes the saved attention outputs cost ~zero GPU memory at the price of CPU RAM and PCIe
traffic, and stacks with `offload.hidden_states` or `offload.all`. It covers everything the
selective policy saves, including saves a plugin requires, such as expert parallelism's routing
decisions. It requires `selective`: without it, those plugin saves stay on GPU.

Requires non-reentrant checkpointing (the default). Composes with `offload.hidden_states` or
`offload.all`: layer inputs go to CPU (with `offload.all`, so does what is saved outside the
layers) while the saved ops' outputs stay on GPU, or go to CPU with `offload.selective: cpu`.
Saving matmul ops (via `save`, `save_modules` or `save_matmul_min_k`) is rejected while a
fused LoRA kernel is enabled, because the kernel adds the adapter delta into the base matmul
output in place, which invalidates the cached tensor.

#### Saving specific projections

All projections dispatch the same `aten::mm`/`aten::addmm`, so `save: [aten::mm]` saves every
one of them. Two rules target individual projections instead; both also work with
`offload.selective: cpu`.

`save_modules` saves the matmuls that run inside the named modules:

```yaml
activation_checkpointing:
  selective:
    save: [attention]
    save_modules: [o_proj]
```

An entry matches a module name exactly, as a trailing dotted suffix (`o_proj`,
`self_attn.o_proj`), or as a glob over the full name when it contains `*`, `?` or `[`. Names are
those of the base model, before PEFT wraps it, and a PEFT-wrapped match resolves to its
`base_layer`, so only the frozen base matmul is saved, not `lora_A`/`lora_B`. Modules that
enclose the decoder layers, or run outside them (`lm_head`, `embed_tokens`), are never in scope.

`save_matmul_min_k` saves every matmul whose contraction dim K (a linear's `in_features`) is at
least the threshold, including MoE expert (`aten::_grouped_mm`) and bitsandbytes 4-bit gemms:

```yaml
activation_checkpointing:
  selective:
    save: [attention]
    save_matmul_min_k: 8192
```

Saving only helps for ops that recompute would otherwise re-run. Recompute stops at the last
tensor backward needs, so a layer's final projection (`down_proj` in Llama/Qwen3-style layers,
whose output only feeds the residual add) is never replayed; saving it costs memory for no
speedup. Prefer `o_proj`, `gate_proj` or `up_proj`.

Validation rejects entries covered by an enabled fused LoRA kernel (`lora_mlp_kernel`,
`lora_qkv_kernel`, `lora_o_kernel`, auto-enabled for LoRA/QLoRA), and the error names the flag
to turn off. At runtime a warning is logged for any rule that matched no module, whose hooks never
fired, whose saved tensors were never replayed, or whose threshold no matmul reached.

`save: []` saves nothing through the list, so `save: []` with `save_modules` saves only the named
projections and recomputes attention.

#### Plugin-registered saves

Plugins can register ops that every selective-checkpoint policy saves, ahead of `save` and the
rules, through `axolotl.monkeypatch.selective_checkpointing`. `register_mandatory_save` is for
correctness: ops whose recompute would diverge from the forward, such as a router's `topk` whose
near-ties would re-route tokens, or a device-to-host copy that sizes a collective and would
re-sync. Their outputs are cloned for the forward so an in-place edit (a router normalising its
`topk` weights) cannot corrupt the cached copy. `register_preferred_save` only trades memory for
skipping an expensive recompute. FSDP2's checkpoint wrapper (`implementation: fsdp`) applies
registered saves on its own; under transformers' checkpointing without `selective`, a plugin
installs them with `apply_selective_checkpointing(model, save=[])`.

### Enabling Layer Offloading

```yaml
layer_offloading: true
```

Layer offloading reduces GPU memory usage by moving frozen (non-trainable) decoder layer parameters to CPU
and streaming them back to GPU one layer at a time during the forward and backward passes. This is
particularly useful for LoRA/QLoRA training where most of the model's parameters are frozen — only the
trainable adapter weights stay on GPU permanently.

During training, forward and backward hooks on each decoder layer handle the transfer automatically:

- **Forward pass:** Before a layer executes, its frozen params are loaded to GPU. The next layer is
  prefetched asynchronously on a separate CUDA stream for overlap.
- **Backward pass:** Same pattern in reverse — the current layer's frozen params are loaded and the
  previous layer is prefetched.

After each layer finishes, its frozen params are offloaded back to CPU pinned memory.

This approach trades some CPU-GPU transfer overhead for significant GPU memory savings — the freed memory
is roughly equal to the size of all frozen parameters across all decoder layers, minus one layer's worth
that is kept on GPU at any given time.

**Requirements:**

- CUDA GPU (CPU-only training is not supported for this feature)
- Works with any HuggingFace model architecture that uses decoder layers (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, etc.)
- Best combined with LoRA/QLoRA where most parameters are frozen

### Migrating from the legacy keys {#sec-migrate-activation-checkpointing}

`gradient_checkpointing`, `gradient_checkpointing_kwargs`, `selective_checkpointing`,
`activation_offloading` and `fsdp_config.activation_checkpointing` are deprecated and will be
removed in a future release. A config that sets them still trains as before: Axolotl rewrites them
into the block at startup and logs a warning that prints the block replacing your values.

Combinations that already failed still fail: disk offload, `selective_checkpointing` or
`activation_offloading: hidden_states` without `gradient_checkpointing`, and
`gradient_checkpointing` together with `fsdp_config.activation_checkpointing`. Setting a
deprecated key next to `activation_checkpointing` is also an error.

| Legacy | Replacement |
|---|---|
| `gradient_checkpointing: true` | `activation_checkpointing: true` |
| `gradient_checkpointing: false` | `activation_checkpointing: false` (the default) |
| `gradient_checkpointing: offload` | `activation_checkpointing: {offload: {all: cpu}}` |
| `gradient_checkpointing_kwargs: {use_reentrant: X}` | `activation_checkpointing: {reentrant: X}` |
| other `gradient_checkpointing_kwargs` keys | `activation_checkpointing.kwargs` (keys that `torch.utils.checkpoint` doesn't accept are dropped with a warning) |
| `gradient_checkpointing_kwargs: {offload: true}` | `activation_checkpointing: {offload: {hidden_states: cpu}}` (stream-overlapped instead of synchronous) |
| `selective_checkpointing: true` or `{...}` | `activation_checkpointing.selective: true` or `{...}` |
| `selective_checkpointing.offload: true` | `activation_checkpointing.offload.selective: cpu` |
| `activation_offloading: true` / `legacy` | `activation_checkpointing.offload.all: cpu` |
| `activation_offloading: true` without `gradient_checkpointing` | `activation_checkpointing: {enabled: false, offload: {all: cpu}}` |
| `activation_offloading: hidden_states` | `activation_checkpointing.offload.hidden_states: cpu` |
| `activation_offloading: disk`, `gradient_checkpointing: offload_disk` | rejected: disk offload is disabled pending a fix (these never wrote to disk; they ran the CPU offloader) |
| `fsdp_config.activation_checkpointing: true` | `activation_checkpointing: {implementation: fsdp}` |
| `gradient_checkpointing: true` and `fsdp_config.activation_checkpointing: true` | rejected, as transformers' Trainer rejected the two together: use `activation_checkpointing: true`, or `{implementation: fsdp}` for FSDP's wrapper |

For example:

```yaml
# before
gradient_checkpointing: true
gradient_checkpointing_kwargs:
  use_reentrant: false
activation_offloading: hidden_states

# after
activation_checkpointing:
  reentrant: false
  offload:
    hidden_states: cpu
```

The CLI flags follow the block: `--activation-checkpointing.enabled`,
`--activation-checkpointing.reentrant`, `--activation-checkpointing.offload.hidden-states`, and so
on. Older Axolotl versions ignore an `activation_checkpointing` key, so a migrated config run on an
older version trains without checkpointing.
